While working as a film programmer or judge at a film festival, he has striven to develop interest in underseen films. He is a particular fan of digging deep into forgotten corners of film history.

Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings trilogy represents some of the finest blockbuster filmmaking of the 21st century. The director’s vision balanced the epic scale of J. R. R. Tolkien’s fantasy saga with a light, humanist touch (as well as plenty of the gross-out jump scares that Jackson mastered with early films like his Muppets parody Meet the Feebles). In the trilogy, the human element is closely tied with the story of the four hobbits who leave their home in the cozy, provincial Shire to face certain death in exchange for defeating the great evils that haunt Middle Earth. The first film of the trilogy, 2001’s Fellowship of the Ring, sets its opening moments in the Shire, and those scenes become very important the further the characters get from home. As the movies go on, the hobbits face monsters, enter war zones, and find themselves spiritually tormented, leaving the Shire as just a memory.

Tolkien’s original Lord of the Rings concluded with a brief fight to reclaim the Shire after it too was sucked into the vortex of war, which was ultimately cut from the films because 2003’s conclusive Return of the King already had a long and unwieldy epilogue. But the novels and the films end the same way, with gardener Samwise Gamgee (Sean Astin) returning to his home after tearfully seeing off Frodo (Elijah Wood), taking in the scene of his wife and children, and saying, “Well, I’m back.” Sam’s famous declaration put the focus of the series ultimately back on the hobbits, on the gravity of returning home after trudging through life-threatening danger for the greater good. Returning to the Shire doesn’t necessarily heal the wounds the characters experienced, or the ones still to come.

blocks.x: While Frodo is the character initially tasked with carrying the One Ring to its resting place in Mount Doom in Fellowship of the Ring, he doesn’t have the combat chops of Legolas (Orlando Bloom) or Gimli (John Rhys-Davies). Nor does he share the hidden dignity of Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen). He’s not a hero but a hobbit, with the weight of the world resting around his neck. When the Fellowship breaks apart after the death of Gandalf (Ian McKellen) in the first film, he and Sam are left to their own devices to trudge through to Mount Doom. The nature of their journey makes the war more abstract for them — they are often too distant from the action to really observe it, with the exception of the climactic moment in The Two Towers in which they have to fight their way through the wartorn Osgiliath.

By the end of Return of the King, the Fellowship has seen it all. Devastation wrought by the forces of Sauron and Saruman (Christopher Lee), the brutal deaths of friends and countrymen, and a victory found at a moment of great desperation. The massive sense of scale in the films is balanced lightly by the horrors of what the characters have seen, and the sense of adventure that is frequently overwhelming to the diminutive hobbits. Sam, tasked with keeping Frodo safe, spends most of the movies fighting with Gollum (Andy Serkis, now directing his own Lord of the Rings film) and keeping the Ring from breaking his best friend’s spirits. The psychological weight of their journey is directly juxtaposed against the Fellowship’s epic adventures.

blocks.x: By the time Frodo eventually succeeds in destroying the Ring (through a nice bit of irony), it’s largely through the help of Sam and the Fellowship’s work from afar. His stature made him a perfect vessel through which the Ring could be destroyed, and the relative reputation of hobbits — the most insular and humble of fantasy races — is kept largely the same by the films’ end. Hobbits are Tolkien’s slight exaggeration of the typical provincial British villager, with an aversion to adventure that is comical and, by the end of the 10-hour film saga, truly poignant. Knowing their distance from home and the weight of their journey, it’s hard not to be moved by their success and the movie’s surprising ambivalence towards their time back, particularly Sam's journey from gardener to savior.

Borrowing from war movies like The Deer Hunter, Peter Jackson keeps the return to the Shire relatively uneasy. After what they’ve experienced, can they truly go back to the Green Dragon for drinks? Can one ever really go back home? Frodo, in particular, seems to feel a profound disconnect from the home he’s returned to, which ultimately leads to his abandoning the Shire for the Undying Lands in the movie’s penultimate scene. That leaves the burden of perspective on Sam, who speaks the movie’s final line upon returning to his family, a perfect and small-scale capper to the fantasy epic. For all the incredible heroism and spectacle of the trilogy, this last moment is the key to its lasting resonance.
